usage: Grep entries by topic to find the exact file and locator for a fact; read the file to verify before citing. Narrative syntheses live in core-lessons.md and history-fingerplays.md; the topic->source workflow lives in retrieval-guide.md.

entries.fact: The body is the first instrument; movement is the pedagogy, not an add-on. Songs are scores for physical action.
entries.quote: movement is a natural response to music

entries.fact: First Steps in Music is an 8-part music-readiness curriculum (3-8 yrs); four of eight parts are movement, including Beat Motion Activities for maintaining the beat in groups of 2 and 3.
Fingerplay songs are fine-motor training for the hand muscles that later hold a pencil.
entries.locator: section 'Music and Movement' (Hannah & Joseph, Where Is Thumbkin vignette)

entries.fact: Kodaly kindergarten analysis sheets classify songs by tone set, rhythm, melodic form, and game type - the game is part of how the music is learned.
entries.quote: Game. Describe the type of game (circle, double circle, partner, double line, follow the leader, etc.)

entries.fact: Singing builds phonological awareness because adults sing to children slower than they speak, letting children hear the smaller parts of words.
entries.quote: we generally sing to children at a slower rate than we speak to them

entries.fact: Rhyming songs let children hear that word-endings can swap; knowing how to rhyme supports later reading success.
entries.locator: section 'Music, Language, and Literacy' (I'm a Little Teapot: stout/spout/shout/out)
entries.quote: Knowing how to rhyme will support later reading success.

entries.fact: Every Child Ready to Read (ALA) names five daily practices for caregivers: Read, Talk, Sing, Write, Play; libraries operationalize Singing through rhymes and songs.
Every saved document is a version of how a song was taught; year/era/region/pedagogy context per file is what shows change over time.
entries.quote: every saved document is a *version* of how a song was taught

entries.fact: The Learning Station repurposed the Itsy Bitsy Spider concept as 'Itsy Ditsy Spider', a breathing/self-regulation meditation - same melody lineage, new purpose.
entries.quote: Each breath says, I am safe and I am calm.

entries.fact: Traditional Itsy Bitsy Spider handouts print size-variation verses (great big giant spider / teeny weeny spider) - built-in mutation.
In the 1843 American Mother Goose chapbook, Pat-a-cake is marked with T 'For Tommy and me' - the letter-swap teaching trick existed 180 years ago.
entries.quote: And mark it with T. / And then it will serve / For Tommy and me.

entries.fact: A 2022 handout teaches the same letter swap: change 'Baby' to 'Mama' and mark it with an M.
Programs are ritualized (Hello/Goodbye songs) and repeat a small repertoire deeply (12 weeks, one Song of the Week); children remember gestures before words.
Storytimes train caregivers via research-based 'early literacy asides'; the adult is the real student so songs reach the home daily.
Froebel's 1844 Mother-Play book ends with 'Notes to Mothers' - the historical original of the modern 'aside to the adult'.
Music is the most adaptable early-years subject: a non-verbal child joins via gesture and humming; a child in a wheelchair leads the parade with a tambourine.
Lullabies and soft singing co-regulate babies and teach emotional self-regulation; strategy songs give toddlers scripts for big feelings.
The highest milestone is the child inventing songs (Anita's doll song, Diego's garbage-truck song); Feierabend names this stage arioso.
entries.quote: Spontaneous created songs by the child

entries.fact: Poulsson (1893) opens by claiming fingerplays are universal and ancient, citing Pat-a-cake and 'Here is the church, here's the steeple' as already-old plays.
entries.quote: In all times and among all nations, finger-plays have been a delight of childhood

entries.fact: Froebel's Mutter- und Kose-Lieder (1844) made folk hand-play intentional pedagogy: finger exercises incl. Pat-a-cake (No.12), This Little Thumb (No.16), The Finger Game, Brothers and Sisters; each play = engraving + song + motto + notes to mothers.
entries.quote: Counting is a noble art, / That man is wont to underrate

entries.fact: The defining Froebelian epigraph: 'What the child imitates, he begins to understand' - imitation of birds, fish, bakers is how the child enters the life of the world.

By 1887 American kindergarten songbooks already had a section titled FINGER PLAYS (Eight white Sheep; Thumbkin says, 'I'll dance.'; The Family; The Little Mice are creeping...) - six years before Poulsson's dedicated book.

Poulsson's 1893 Finger Plays for Nursery and Kindergarten is the first book devoted to the form; its title page registers 'FINGER PLAYS' as a U.S. trademark - the term was a coined commercial category.
Poulsson's preface gives the first plain developmental rationale: strength and flexibility of 'the tiny lax fingers', and motions that awaken dormant thought.
entries.quote: the development of strength and flexibility in the tiny lax fingers

entries.fact: Quigley's 1914 Index to Kindergarten Songs lists Pat-a-cake across Froebel, Gaynor, Hubbard, Smith and Brewster - the canon hardened across five independent songbooks.

Victorian folklorists (Gomme 1894/98, Newell 1883/1903, Green 1899) collected children's hand-games (Handy Dandy, Chickidy Hand) as survivals of ancient custom - treating clapping games as historical sources.
entries.locator: game index (Chickidy Hand, Handy Dandy, Hand in and Hand out)

entries.fact: Traceable lineage: Froebel 'This Little Thumb' (No.16) -> Jenks 'Thumbkin says, I'll dance.' (1887) -> modern 'Where Is Thumbkin?' in library booklets and Head Start.
entries.locator: glob song_versions/*thumbkin*; see history-fingerplays.md lineages table

entries.fact: The stated why of fingerplays shifts over time while the form stays constant: 1844 cosmic/theological unity -> 1893 finger strength and awakened thought -> 1990s-2020s fine-motor skills, phonological awareness, self-regulation.
Steady-beat teaching for ages 2-7 uses clapping patterns (Pat-a-cake), marching songs (Ants Go Marching), tempo play (Polly Wolly Doodle), and DIY rain sticks.
Head Start recommends the adult's live voice over recordings: the adult sings slower and clearer and can adapt tone, speed, and volume to the child.
entries.locator: section 'Using Music with Infants and Toddlers' (Janet vignette)

entries.fact: To find where a song version came from: glob song_versions/<slug>*.md, read frontmatter (source_file, source_title, confidence, review_status), then cross-reference MASTER_LIST.md and metadata/<folder>.md for url/year/era/region.
